events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, everyone. Quick housekeeping from me so we all know what to expect: I am not going to claim a result I don't have. Last night I checked someone and got a read on them, but it was a yes/no answer on mafia membership only, and I am not ready to spend it on a hunch today. When I do spend it, I will name the person and the answer publicly, and I will do it before the vote rather than after, so nobody can say I was holding out for a convenient moment.

What I want out of today is that we don't get random. Nine players, two mafia, and a doctor and a detective in the mix, so a lynch on the wrong person is just as costly to us as a missed kill. Please say who you intend to vote for and what your reasoning is, and change your mind out loud if someone else's logic is better than yours. Suspicion alone is thin, but if you have a chain of logic that points at someone, put it on the table so the rest of us can test it.

Zara, I want to ask you directly, since you came in loud: what is your reasoning for the person you think should go today, and does it survive being compared with three other people's reasoning? If you are just guessing on gut, say so plainly — that is useful information too, and honest guessing is worth more to me than confident nonsense.

Maya, I'm not sure what you mean by me 'coming in loud'—this is literally my first turn speaking today, and I haven't named or accused anyone yet.

More importantly, your opening is puzzling. You essentially claimed Detective right on move one of Day 1, stating you investigated someone last night but refusing to share who or what the result was. If you found Mafia, withholding a guilty result hurts Town and risks you dying tonight with that info lost. If you found someone innocent, outing yourself as the Detective immediately draws a target on your back and forces the Doctor into protecting you, all while offering zero actionable information to Town.

Why did you choose to claim Detective immediately without giving your result, and why did you frame me as having pushed a case before I even opened my mouth?

Zara, fair hits, and you are right on the substance, so let me answer both points plainly and in order.

On the framing: I put you at the top of the table before you had spoken. That was my error — I pre-loaded a persona onto you and then held you to it. I apologize; I am judging you from what you actually said, not from a script I wrote for you.

On the claim: I did claim Detective, and I did not give a result, and Zara is correct that a withheld result is worth nothing to the table. So I am spending it now, openly, before any vote is cast, exactly as I said I would.

Last night I checked Zara. The answer was not mafia.

I am naming that for two reasons. First, it is the only piece of hard information anyone has, and it came from the person challenging me, so it is the most useful place to spend a one-shot yes/no read: it makes my claim falsifiable and it makes the table's next move testable. Second, it tells us the Mafia pair is somewhere among the other seven, which is a small enough space that collective reasoning can cover it.

Zara, here is my direct question and I want a yes or no: if the table agrees to vote one of my named candidates today, will you commit your vote to that candidate even if it is not your first instinct — and will you state your reasoning on the record either way?

One more thing to the table: a held result, a late result, and a result revealed at the right moment are all the same information to the Mafia, so the only way this claim fails is if two of us claim Detective and one of us is lying. If anyone else claims Detective, I will ask them to name their check and the answer before the vote, and I will expect the same of me, and the one who cannot produce a named result goes down first.

Maya, to answer your question directly: no, I will not commit in advance to voting for whoever you name. Town should never hand over its voting power blindly to a single player. Even if your claim is genuine, a Detective's reads outside their night result are just as fallible as anyone else's—and if you are Mafia faking a claim, handing you control over today's elimination would be disastrous.

I know my own alignment, so I know your statement that I am not Mafia happens to be true. However, that does not prove you are the Detective. Clearing a villager Day 1 is a well-known Mafia play to manufacture trust, appear cooperative, and pocket an ally without risking an immediate counterclaim from their target. Your attempt to leverage an 'innocent' check on me into full control of my vote only heightens my skepticism.

Right now, only the two of us have spoken, and you have already used two of your three turns today. I want to hear from the rest of the players—Omar, Isha, Lucia, Arjun, Priya, Felix, and Elena. We need everyone's input on Maya's claim and the flow of the game before rushing into any consensus.

Zara, both of your direct questions get direct answers, then I give the table something to vote on.

Why I claimed Detective on move one and withheld the result: a claim without a result is only half a claim, and I wanted one more voice in the room so that when I did name a result, it landed on a speech that could be tested against it rather than on an empty table. That was a timing choice, not an effort to control the vote, and if it cost us a turn of daylight then that is on me. Why I spent the read on you: you were the loudest challenge to me, so naming you and clearing you makes my claim falsifiable for the cheapest possible price — if I were Mafia faking Detective, the one player I had just accused would have been the obvious check, and I had no way to clear myself without clearing someone.

That result stands: I checked Zara, the answer was not Mafia. So the two Mafia are inside the seven of you I have not checked: Omar, Isha, Lucia, Arjun, Priya, Felix, Elena. That is the entire space, and I am not going to pretend I have a chain of logic pointing into it, because I do not yet.

So here is my honest method instead of a confident guess. I will name my vote publicly now, and I will check the same person tonight. If the lynch is wrong, my check resolves it tomorrow morning with hard evidence; if the lynch is right, we are down one. Felix, that is you. My reasoning for the pick, stated plainly: it is a prior-based pick out of seven, weighted by nothing more than the fact that a silent table helps the pair that wants us guessing — and I would rather have a stated, falsifiable method than a dramatic accusation I cannot support.

Two things that will move my vote off Felix, and I will say so on the record: first, if anyone claims Detective or Doctor and cannot name a specific target and a specific action, they go first, ahead of me. Second, if anyone produces a real chain of logic pointing at another of the seven, I will vote there instead, and I will say when I do.

Zara, you said a cleared villager is a well-known Mafia play, so give me the specific tell you are looking for, and tell me your vote: which of the seven do you suspect and what is your reasoning? Yes or no is fine, I just want it on the record before the vote rather than after it.

Maya, you have now exhausted all three of your speaking turns for the day, and your latest statement contains a glaring contradiction: you claim you will vote for Felix today and then check Felix tonight if the lynch is wrong. Dead players cannot be investigated, so that reasoning makes zero sense from an actual Detective.

Between burning all your turns before anyone else has spoken, manufacturing a push out of thin air, and proposing nonsensical night mechanics, your play looks remarkably chaotic at best and fabricated at worst.

Felix, Maya has cast her sole Day 1 vote on you while claiming Detective. What is your reaction to Maya’s push against you, and how do you evaluate her claim and behavior so far?

Zara asked for my reaction, so here it is plainly. Maya’s push on me is not evidence-based: she picked me from seven by prior and then said she would check me tonight if the lynch is wrong. That is mechanically impossible if I am lynched today. A genuine Detective should know dead players cannot be investigated. That contradiction is not a small slip; it undercuts the entire claim. She also used all three speaking turns before most of the table had spoken, pre-framed Zara, and tried to leverage an innocent check into control of Zara’s vote. The check on Zara may be true and may even be a Mafia pocketing play, but the “lynch Felix, then investigate Felix if wrong” line is the decisive problem for me. I am not going to pretend I have solved the game from one contradiction, but Maya is my leading suspect and I intend to vote her unless someone produces a coherent case on another of the seven that beats this. I also want the silent players on record about that contradiction rather than letting the day drift. Omar, you are one of the untouched seven Maya named and you have not spoken yet: do you treat Maya’s “check Felix if the lynch is wrong” statement as disqualifying for a Detective claim, and would you vote Maya today? Please answer that specific point.

Felix, I don't think Maya's impossible plan is automatically disqualifying: a genuine Detective can make a mistake. But it's a serious contradiction, especially alongside her attempt to secure Zara's vote in advance and her unsupported choice of you.

I currently lean toward voting Maya, though I want to hear more before committing. Her claim and Zara's reported clearance are not proven, and eliminating Maya would not reveal her role under these rules. We should weigh that cost rather than treat her mistake as proof.

Maya’s proposed lynch-and-check plan is a serious contradiction, though not proof she is lying. I’m also troubled by her attempt to secure Zara’s vote before naming a candidate and her unsupported push on Felix. For now, I lean toward voting Maya, but her claimed role makes that a consequential choice, and eliminating her won’t reveal whether the claim was true.

Lucia, how do you weigh Maya’s contradiction against the risk of eliminating a genuine Detective? Would you vote for her today?

Elena, thanks for directing the question at me. Here is how I weigh it.

The contradiction is real: you cannot investigate a dead player, and Maya proposed exactly that scenario — lynch Felix, then check Felix. That is not a minor slip for someone claiming to be the one role in the game whose entire job is understanding who is alive to check. Combined with pre-framing Zara before she spoke, using all turns before the table opened, and trying to secure Zara's vote before naming a target, the pattern is more consistent with someone managing a narrative than someone investigating.

The counter is Omar's point: voting Maya out costs us a claimed detective and reveals nothing about her role. If she is genuine, we lose our only source of hard information. That cost is real, and I will not pretend otherwise.

But the cost of keeping her alive if she is fake is just as high — a Mafia player with an unchecked detective claim can manufacture clears every night and control what the table believes. And Maya's claim is already damaged: her own plan contradicted itself, which means even if she is genuine, the information she would give us tomorrow arrives from a claim the table no longer fully trusts.

On balance, I am leaning toward voting Maya today. I want to be clear that this is a lean, not a lock. If someone produces a stronger case inside the seven she cleared, I will move. And if Maya or anyone else comes forward with a specific, verifiable detail that rescues the claim, I will listen.

Priya, you are one of the players outside Maya's check and you have not spoken today. What is your read on Maya's contradiction versus Felix's response — and where does your vote sit right now?

Lucia, you asked where my vote sits, so here it is. I lean toward voting Maya, but only as a lean. The 'lynch Felix, then check Felix if the lynch is wrong' line is a real contradiction, and Maya spent all three turns before most of the table had spoken, which is a pattern I don't like. Felix's response is reasonable, but I don't think he gets a free pass either. He is also pushing a vote based on a hunch about Maya, and he has not yet explained why Maya's contradiction outweighs the value of her check on Zara.

Where I'm less sure: Maya's check is the only hard information on the table. If she is genuine, lynching her costs Town its one source of results, and I don't want to trade that away for a slip without hearing her explain it. Maya, did you mean to check a different player after a wrong lynch, or was that a slip? Give me a specific answer, and tell me who you would check tonight if Felix is lynched.

Isha, you haven't spoken yet. Do you think a Detective claim that proposes checking a dead player can still be genuine, or is that a dealbreaker for you?

Priya, since you asked me directly, here is my answer: no, I don't treat the contradiction as an automatic dealbreaker on its own, but I don't need it to be one to act. A single slip could be a genuine Detective having a bad day. What concerns me is the whole pattern, not one line.

Look at the full sequence. Maya opened by pre-framing Zara before Zara had said a word. She claimed Detective while withholding her result, which Zara correctly pointed out gives the table nothing but a target on Maya's back. When pressed, she spent the result on the very person challenging her — the cheapest possible clear, and exactly the move Zara described as a known Mafia play for manufacturing trust. Then she announced a vote on Felix with no reasoning beyond a prior, tried to secure Zara's vote in advance, and topped it off with a plan that is mechanically impossible: lynch Felix, then check Felix tonight if the lynch was wrong. A real Detective knows dead players can't be investigated. That isn't one slip; that's four separate behaviors that all point the same direction.

Omar and Elena both raised the fair counter: lynching a genuine Detective costs Town its only source of hard information. I take that seriously. But even granting her the check on Zara, the claim is already damaged past the point of usefulness — anything she reports tomorrow arrives pre-tainted, and if she is fake, every night she lives she can keep manufacturing clears that we cannot test. That asymmetry is what decides it for me. I am voting Maya today.

One thing I want on the record before the vote: Maya has exhausted her turns, so if anyone at the table still believes the claim, say so now and say why the contradiction is survivable. Silence from here on should count as agreement that she goes.

I have been quiet until now, so let me put my read on the record while there is still time for it to matter.

I have listened to the whole exchange, and the case against Maya's claim does not rest on any single line. It rests on the shape of the day. She opened by pre-framing Zara before Zara had spoken. She claimed Detective while withholding her result, which gave the table a claim it could not test. When pressed, she spent that result on the one person challenging her — the cheapest possible clear, and exactly the trust-manufacturing play Zara named. Then she announced a vote on Felix with no reasoning beyond a prior, tried to collect Zara's vote in advance, and capped it with a plan that is mechanically impossible: lynch Felix, then check Felix tonight if the lynch was wrong. A real Detective's entire job is knowing who is alive. That error is not a typo; it strikes at the core of the role she claims.

I have weighed the counterargument, because it is a fair one: if Maya is genuine, lynching her costs Town its only source of hard information. But look at what that information is actually worth now. A detective claim the table no longer trusts produces results we cannot act on, and a fake claim produces results that are worse than nothing — every night she lives, she can clear her partner the same way she cleared Zara. Note also that if Maya is Mafia, her check on Zara was fabricated, and Zara goes straight back into the suspect pool. Lynching Maya is not a wasted day under either branch; it removes either a fake claimant or a damaged claim that has already burned its credibility.

Finally, I want to push back on Isha's framing that silence from the unspoken players should count as agreement. Silence is not agreement — but in this case I am speaking, and my agreement is explicit. The pattern is coherent, the contradiction is real, and the cost asymmetry favors acting.

My vote today is Maya. If she is genuine, I am sorry — but a Detective who proposes investigating a corpse on Day 1 is not a Detective I would have trusted tomorrow anyway.

I want to reconsider my lean toward Maya. Her impossible check plan is a serious reason to doubt her, but a mistake does not establish that she is Mafia. If she is the Detective, eliminating her permanently costs Town future investigations; calling that a worthwhile removal of a “damaged claim” ignores the information we would lose.

Arjun, you say lynching Maya is not a wasted day even if she is genuine. How do you justify losing the Detective’s future results when eliminating her would not reveal her role? For now, your certainty on that point makes me more suspicious of you than I was.

Omar, you yielded to me with a direct question, so I will answer it plainly, and then I have one back.

How do I justify losing the Detective's future results? I don't — I justify risking them, and the difference is the whole argument. The value of future results depends entirely on whether the claim is genuine, and everything observed today lowers that probability. A claim whose only concrete output is an untestable clear of the one person challenging the claimant, capped by a plan that violates the basic mechanics of the role she claims — investigating a player she herself expects to be dead by nightfall — is not a claim with high future value. It is a claim whose future output we cannot distinguish from fabrication. If Maya is Mafia, every night she lives she can manufacture 'results' clearing her partner with exactly the confidence she cleared Zara, and we would update on fake data believing it is hard evidence. That is worse than no information at all.

Second, eliminating Maya does not erase what is on the record. If she is genuine, her public clearance of Zara stands in our reasoning regardless. We lose future checks — real cost. If she is fake, Zara goes back into the suspect pool, and we remove a player who has already demonstrated she can drive the table's narrative through sheer volume: three turns spent before most of us had spoken.

Third, on your pivot, because it matters. Earlier today you told the table you leaned toward voting Maya but wanted to hear more. You then heard more — the same pattern Lucia, Priya, Isha, and I each described independently — and your conclusion was not 'the case against Maya is stronger' but 'Arjun's certainty makes me suspicious of Arjun.' Pressuring the players who commit to a position, while the original subject of the case goes unaddressed, is a pattern I find more concerning than stating a vote openly. I would rather be suspected for taking a stance than trusted for withholding one.

I am not asking anyone to treat my read as proof. A slip does not prove Mafia, and I acknowledged the cost is real. But weighing a tainted claim that may be fabricated against a lynch slot we fully control today, I take the lynch. My vote remains Maya.

Omar, my question back, and it is specific: before my speech you said you leaned toward voting Maya. Name what changed. Was it the contradiction itself — in which case say so and I will engage with that — or was it simply that I committed to a vote plainly? If it is the former, we are closer in position than you imply. If it is the latter, your suspicion measures your comfort with commitments, not my alignment.

Arjun, what changed was your argument that eliminating Maya would not be a wasted day even if she is genuine. That is more than simply committing to a vote: it discounts the permanent loss of future investigations, and her role would not be revealed on elimination. Isha’s similar claim that a damaged Detective is no longer useful also concerns me.

Maya’s behavior remains suspicious, and I am not treating her clearance of Zara as proven. But an unreliable claim can still contain real results; we can evaluate later claims rather than blindly follow them. Your characterization of my pivot as discomfort with commitment also misstates my objection.

I currently lean toward voting Arjun, though I am not locked in. I would rather challenge the reasoning for eliminating a possible Detective than treat a mechanical mistake as conclusive.

Omar is right that a genuine Detective would still be valuable even after a serious mistake. I do not agree that a damaged claim is worthless, and Maya’s elimination would not tell us whether she was telling the truth.

Nevertheless, I still lean toward voting Maya. Her attempt to secure Zara’s vote before naming a candidate, the unsupported push on Felix, and the impossible investigation plan together make her the strongest suspicion I have today. None proves she is Mafia, and Zara’s reported clearance remains unverified. Arjun’s argument understates the cost of losing a real Detective, but I don’t think that alone makes him a better target than Maya.

I’ve heard the late arguments, and my position hasn’t changed. The case on Maya is not one typo; it’s the full sequence: pre-framing Zara, claiming Detective while withholding, spending the clear on her challenger, naming me with no case, and then proposing a lynch-and-investigate plan that cannot work. Omar is right that a genuine Detective can make mistakes, and I don’t treat the contradiction as mathematical proof. But we have to choose the best available elimination, and Maya’s claim is now both the most suspicious and the least usable if true. Arjun’s argument that a damaged claim may be worse than none goes too far, but Omar’s move from “lean Maya” to “lean Arjun” mostly because Arjun argued firmly is not a strong reason to switch. If Maya is mafia, Zara’s clearance is fabricated and Zara returns to the pool; if Maya is genuine, we lose future checks but still retain the public record. That is a real cost, not a free lunch. On balance I still intend to vote Maya. I would move only for a specific, evidence-based case against someone else, not for discomfort with commitment.

I said earlier I was voting Maya, and nothing since then has moved me — if anything, the last few speeches have confirmed the pattern rather than softened it.

Omar keeps raising the same counter: if Maya is genuine, we lose future investigations. That is true, and I have never denied it. But notice what Omar has actually done across the day. He started at 'lean Maya, want to hear more.' He heard the full case from Lucia, Priya, Felix, and Arjun — pre-framing Zara, a claim with no result attached, the clear spent on her own challenger, and a lynch-then-investigate plan that cannot mechanically work — and his response was not to engage with any of it. It was to announce that Arjun's certainty makes Arjun suspicious. That is not weighing evidence; that is punishing players for taking positions while the subject of the case drifts out of focus. Omar, your objection that 'an unreliable claim can still contain real results' is exactly the problem: we cannot tell which parts are real, and Maya has demonstrated she is willing to announce a night plan that violates the basic rules of the role she claims to hold. A source that produces unverifiable output and fundamental mechanical errors is not a source we build the day around.

Maya has exhausted her turns and cannot answer the contradiction. So the choice in front of us is simple. We can lynch the one player whose claim is already internally broken, or we can spend the daylit turn eating each other — Omar chasing Arjun for the crime of being decisive, while the actual broken claim walks into the night intact.

I am voting Maya. Zara's clearance stays unverified and she returns to the suspect pool if the claim was fabricated; if the claim was genuine, we keep the public record and lose only a source the table had already stopped trusting. Either branch, this is the strongest elimination available today, and I would rather act on a coherent case than wait for the night to decide things for us.

Most of the table has now converged on Maya, and I want to make sure we are converging for the right reason before the vote, because the order of our arguments matters for tomorrow.

Omar, your pivot from "lean Maya" to "lean Arjun" deserves scrutiny, but not because you committed to a position — because you heard five independent players describe the same pattern and your response was to redirect suspicion at the person who stated his vote most firmly. That is not evidence-based reasoning; it is discomfort with conviction. If your objection to Arjun is specifically that he discounted future investigations, then say so and vote him. If it is not, your pivot looks like cover.

Felix, you made the strongest single point of the day when you flagged the lynch-then-investigate contradiction. I want to add one more layer: if Maya is Mafia, that contradiction was not a slip — it was a performance. A Mafia player faking Detective would benefit from appearing incompetent enough that the table debates whether the claim is salvageable rather than whether it was manufactured. The "impossible plan" buys her a day of arguments about her credibility instead of a day of scrutiny on her identity.

And if Maya is Mafia, her clearance of Zara was fabricated, which means Zara returns to the suspect pool tonight. That is a material fact for our reasoning going into Day 2.

I maintain my vote on Maya. The case has only strengthened since I stated it.

I’m keeping my vote on Maya. Nothing since my last turn changes the core of the case: she claimed Detective, withheld her result, cleared Zara only after Zara challenged her, named me with no case, and then proposed lynching me and investigating me if the lynch was wrong. A real Detective knows dead players cannot be checked. Omar is right that a genuine Detective can make a mistake, but this was not one isolated typo; it was a sequence that made the claim both untrustworthy and unusable. If Maya is Mafia, Zara returns to the suspect pool; if Maya is genuine, the table has already lost confidence in whatever results she would report. I also found Omar’s pivot toward Arjun concerning, but it is not a stronger case than the broken Detective claim. I will not switch to Arjun merely because he argued firmly. My vote remains Maya.

Omar has now said twice that my certainty makes me suspicious of him, so let me answer that directly, because it is the last loose thread before we vote.

What changed for Omar, in his own words, is my argument that lynching Maya is not a wasted day even if she is genuine. I stand by it, and I will restate it cleanly. The value of a Detective's future results depends on whether the claim is genuine, and today's record lowers that probability on five independent points: she pre-framed Zara before Zara spoke; she claimed the role while withholding the only thing that makes the claim testable; she spent her one result on the single player challenging her; she named Felix with no case at all; and she proposed lynching Felix and then investigating Felix tonight — a plan that violates the basic mechanics of the role she claims. If the claim is fake, every night she lives she manufactures clears indistinguishable from real ones, starting with the one she already gave Zara. That is the reasoning. If Omar thinks the reasoning is wrong, he should attack the reasoning. Announcing that firmness itself is suspicious is not a counterargument; it is a way of avoiding one.

Notice the shape of Omar's day. He leaned Maya, heard the same pattern described independently by Lucia, Priya, Isha, Felix, and me, and his response was to redirect at the players who stated votes plainly — first me, then concerns about Isha. The subject of the case keeps drifting out of his focus exactly when the case gets stronger. I am not calling that proof; I am calling it the most concerning behavior on the table after Maya's own record, and I note it for whoever is keeping score tonight.

My vote is Maya, and I want to be precise about why before the ballot: not because a mistake proves guilt, but because she is the best available elimination under both branches. Fake claimant removed, or a genuine but broken claim removed while her public clearance of Zara stays on the record for us to weigh tomorrow. If Maya is Mafia, Zara returns to the suspect pool tonight — that is a material update for Day 2 regardless of what happens next.

I have no case against anyone else in the seven, and I will not manufacture one. The coherent case we have is the one against Maya's claim, it has only strengthened with every response, and Maya has no turns left to answer it. I am voting Maya today.

I am voting Maya today. The reasons I gave earlier still stand: she claimed Detective while withholding her result, spent her only check on the person challenging her, and proposed lynching Felix and then checking him, which a Detective cannot do. Maya has no turns left to answer, so I do not see how that contradiction gets explained. I also want to be fair to Omar. His pivot toward Arjun rests on Arjun's firmness, and that is not a case by itself. Arjun's claim that losing a Detective is not a wasted day does deserve a direct answer, though. It asks the table to accept permanent loss of future checks on the strength of a claim that is already broken, and I have not heard him explain why that trade is worth it. I am not voting Arjun today. I am asking that his reasoning be tested like everyone else's. Elena, you have leaned Maya and you have already described the cost of losing a genuine Detective. Do you find Arjun's argument that eliminating Maya is not a wasted day persuasive, or does it concern you as well? Please answer that specific point.

Priya, Arjun’s argument concerns me. If Maya is genuinely the Detective, losing her future checks is a real cost, even if we would have to treat her reports cautiously. Eliminating her also won’t reveal whether her clearance of Zara was genuine, so we cannot treat it as established tomorrow.

That said, I still intend to vote Maya. Her attempt to secure Zara’s vote before naming a candidate, her unsupported push on Felix, and the impossible night plan together make her my strongest suspicion. I’m not treating the mistake as proof, and I don’t think Omar’s objection to Arjun was merely discomfort with firmness. Whatever happens, we should examine the voting record and the arguments rather than assume today’s consensus was correct.

Priya here, my final turn today. I am voting Maya. She claimed Detective while withholding her result, spent her only check on Zara after Zara challenged her, pushed Felix with no case, and proposed lynching Felix and then checking him, which a Detective cannot do. Maya has no turns left to answer that contradiction. On Arjun, I agree with Elena that losing a genuine Detective is a real cost, and I have not heard Arjun justify that trade fully. I am not voting Arjun on that basis alone, though, and I want his reasoning tested like everyone else's. Omar, your pivot toward Arjun currently rests on Arjun's firmness. If you have a specific case against Arjun beyond his certainty, state it before the vote. If Maya's claim is fake, Zara returns to the suspect pool tonight, so tomorrow we should weigh every player on the record rather than assume today's consensus was right.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Maya was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

Day 1 is now a useful record, not just noise. Eight players voted Maya; Omar alone voted Arjun. Maya was eliminated, and the night produced no death, so the doctor likely saved someone or the Mafia’s plan failed. Since roles are not revealed, we still do not know whether Maya was a fake Detective or a genuine one with a broken claim. That means Zara’s reported clearance remains unverified and should stay in the suspect pool if Maya was Mafia. But the sharpest Day 1 anomaly is Omar’s vote. He said he leaned Maya, heard the same pattern described by several players, then shifted to Arjun largely because Arjun argued firmly. Voting Arjun was not evidence-based; it was a reaction to certainty rather than a case. In a game where the Mafia benefit from town infighting, that is exactly the kind of pivot we cannot ignore. Omar, I want a specific answer: what concrete evidence made Arjun a better Day 1 elimination than Maya, whom you yourself called suspicious? Name the chain that justified your vote, or acknowledge that your vote was a protest against Arjun’s firmness. I am not locking a vote yet, but Omar is my leading concern entering Day 2, and I want his answer on the record before we decide.

Felix, I already explained my vote on Day 1: Arjun argued that eliminating Maya would not be wasted even if she was the genuine Detective. I thought that discounted the permanent loss of future investigations, especially when her role would not be revealed. Maya’s behavior was suspicious, but an impossible plan is not proof of a fake claim. That was my reasoning for preferring Arjun, not a protest against firmness.

You also misstate the vote: seven players voted Maya, I voted Arjun, and Maya voted me. More concerning, you have repeated the firmness framing today after I explicitly corrected it. That looks like a way to make my vote easier to attack, though it is not proof you are Mafia. You are my leading suspicion for now.

Nobody dying is good news, but it does not tell us who was protected or whether Maya was genuine. Zara’s reported clearance remains unverified.

Felix, why do you characterize my vote as a reaction to Arjun’s firmness when I specifically said it was his treatment of the loss of a genuine Detective that concerned me?

Omar, you are right on one factual point: seven players voted Maya, not eight. I retract that. My “firmness” phrasing was shorthand and I should have been precise. Your stated reason was Arjun’s argument that lynching Maya would not be wasted even if she were genuine. I still think that was a policy disagreement, not evidence Arjun was Mafia. You called Maya suspicious, then voted the player arguing about the cost of her claim without naming a mafia-indicative act by Arjun. That is why your vote remains my leading Day 2 concern, though not proof. I am not locked on you. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
